newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Ozone hole has never been bigger, convention told.
newsitem.headline: Ozone hole has never been bigger, convention told.

text.p: The hole in the ozone layer over the South Pole grew to its largest size in history in 1996, a meteorological expert said on Wednesday at the world Ozone Summit in San Jose.

"In the second half of September and the beginning of October of 1996, the size of the ozone hole in Antarctica surpassed 22 million square kilometres (8.5 million square miles)," G.O.P. Obasi, secretary-general of the United Nations' World Meteorological Organisation, told about 800 delegates from 160 countries at the three-day meeting.
The size of the hole is equivalent to twice the surface of Europe from the Atlantic Ocean to the Ural Mountains.
Obasi said ozone was being depleted at an unprecedented rate, with none left at a height of 15 to 21 km (9 to 13 miles) for several weeks beginning in the second half of September.

Obasi said worldwide measurements made in Canada, Central Europe and Japan by the World Ozone Observation System showed that in the stratosphere, ozone had been depleted in the last 20 years by close to 1 percent a year at a height of 16 to 22 km (10 to 14 miles).
Ozone depletion increases the Earth's exposure to harmful ultraviolet radiation, which has been linked to skin cancer in humans.

U.S. company 3M Pharmaceuticals, in a report to the conference that cited U.S. government figures, said the ozone layer could well be depleted by 40 percent by 2075, causing an additional 154 million cases of skin cancer and 3.4 million more deaths in the United States.
The Costa Rica meeting, which ends on Wednesday, brings together signatories of the 1987 Montreal Protocol and the 1985 Vienna Convention.

The protocol, ratified by at least 150 countries, called for the gradual phasing out of ozone-depleting substances and established a fund to encourage technology transfer and a switch to less harmful substances.
The convention set up a framework for reducing production of chemicals that deplete the ozone layer, including chlorofluorocarbons, which are widely used in refrigeration and aerosols.
